checkpoints: Nullability is part of the TYPE, not a decorative detail: non-null is a promise of presence, nullable means null is a valid value.
Runtime consequence: a non-null field whose resolver returns null gets converted into an error and null-bubbles up to the nearest nullable parent.
One wrong field can nullify a whole branch, even the entire response.
Per-field decision rule: only declare non-null when the value ALWAYS exists (like id, title, author on Book — always present once the book is created).
Declare nullable when absence is a legitimate state (an unknown publication year).
When absence is exceptional (a book not found on a root field like book(id): Book!), keep the field non-null and throw a typed domain exception instead of silently returning null.
That typed exception passes through the central error-handling point, which maps it into the error envelope with a stable code.
Client angle: tooling reads nullability to generate code — it's a public contract, not a style choice.
N+1 is not a schema-declaration bug — it's a consequence of how GraphQL EXECUTES: the authors resolver is called once for N authors, then the books field resolver is called once PER author.
If each of those per-author calls goes straight to the data source, you get N child lookups plus 1 root lookup — N+1.

The batching data loader mechanism: the field resolver calls load(key), which does NOT run right away — it only registers the key into a queue and returns a promise/future, deferred to a batch boundary (an event-loop tick or equivalent dispatch point).

Once the batch boundary arrives, the loader calls exactly ONE batch function with ALL collected keys, producing a single combined lookup (e.g. WHERE id IN (...)), then distributes results back to each caller.
Constraint: the batch function must return results in the SAME ORDER as the input keys, so it must re-map by key (keys.map(k => resultMap.get(k))) rather than rely on the data source's return order.

Per-request cache: if the same key is load-ed multiple times within one request, the second call reads from the cache without touching the data source again — batching solves width (many keys collapsed into one round), the cache solves depth (duplicate asks for one key).
The cache must live exactly as long as one request's lifecycle, dying when the request ends — otherwise one request's data could leak into another request or user.

None of this is Node-specific or tied to one framework: DataLoader, BatchLoader/DataLoaderRegistry, Hot Chocolate's generated DataLoader, and dataloaden/dataloadgen are all just implementations of the same idea — defer to a collapse point, merge keys into one lookup, cache within one request's scope.

A persisted-query hash is only meaningful as a content identifier - the hash-to-query mapping is trustworthy only when the server itself proves hash equals SHA-256(query) at registration time, rather than accepting whatever pairing a client asserts.

In this implementation, the register endpoint calls `store.set(body.hash, body.query)` directly on unverified client input; because registration now happens outside Apollo's `persistedQueries.cache.set`, Apollo's own built-in hash-matches-query verification never runs at all.

Since the store never checks that the hash matches the query, any client can register an attacker-chosen query under a hash the legitimate app is already known to send hash-only, overwriting or seeding that exact cache entry.

Once a malicious pair is registered, every subsequent hash-only request from real clients - including the official app itself - resolves to and executes the attacker's query instead of the original one, turning a bandwidth optimization into a remote-injection primitive that redirects an entire population of well-behaved callers without touching their code.

The minimum fix is to recompute `sha256(query)` on every store write and reject the request (4xx) when it doesn't equal the supplied hash, which restores exactly the guarantee Apollo's built-in persisted-query cache already provides, making the custom register endpoint unnecessary in favor of the standard protocol.

A stronger posture removes client-driven registration entirely: a build-time trusted-documents allowlist generates the hash-to-query manifest from the client's real query set ahead of time, so the server only ever executes pre-approved hashes and never accepts a query string from a request.

The store backing this registry is an unbounded Map with no TTL or eviction, so junk registrations let it grow forever with no way to bound memory or age out stale entries, compounding the security risk with a resource-growth issue.

Correctness here is proven by tests showing a mismatched hash/query pair is rejected without altering the existing entry for that hash, a legitimate register-then-hash-only round trip still resolves, and repeated junk registrations cannot evict or replace a known-good mapping.

A batching data loader only collapses keys that get registered within the same event-loop tick (the batch dispatch window) into one call; once that window closes, any further `load()` calls open a new window of their own.

Awaiting a `load()` call inside a `for...of` loop fully pauses that iteration until the promise resolves, so the next iteration's `load()` call happens on a later tick — this closes the batch window after exactly one key every time, even though the loader's batch function and scope are configured correctly.

N single-key batch lines in the data-source log (`[BATCH] ... IN ('<one-id>')` repeated N times) instead of one combined multi-key line is the fingerprint of broken batching — it is N+1 in disguise, N sequential round-trips happening despite a batching loader being wired up.

The root cause lives in the calling code's control flow, not in the loader's configuration: the loader itself, its batch function, and its request scope are not the source of the bug, so 'fixing' the loader's setup would not resolve the slowdown.

The fix is to register every `load()` call before awaiting any of them, so all keys land in the same tick: mapping over the collection to start every `load()` synchronously and only then awaiting them together (e.g. with a single combined wait over all the pending calls) lets the loader batch them into one `IN (...)` query.

Turning the related field into its own field resolver that returns the loader's pending call directly, without an `await` inside that resolver, is the more idiomatic fix — the GraphQL engine itself invokes that field once per parent within the same execution tick, so all the resulting `load()` calls naturally land in the same batch window without any manual `Promise.all`.

The loader's per-request cache deduplicates a key that gets loaded twice within the same request, but that is a separate mechanism from batching by width; since every key in this scenario is unique, the cache cannot mask or fix a sequential-await bug like this one.

Proving the fix requires counting batch-log lines for the same nested query before and after (N single-key lines collapsing to one multi-key line) and re-measuring latency against the size of the parent list (linear growth flattening out), then locking in a regression test that asserts exactly one batch-log line per relation per request so the sequential-await bug cannot silently return.

APQ's payoff is amortisation: after a one-time round trip where the client registers the full query and receives a hash back, every subsequent call sends only a 64-character SHA-256 hash instead of the full query text.

That payoff only holds if a registered hash means something the whole fleet agrees on. `PersistedQueryStore.store` is a plain `Map` living in a single NestJS process's heap, so a hash set by one replica is invisible to the `Map` instances running in the other replicas.

With 4 replicas behind round-robin routing and no shared cache, a hash registered on one replica is recognized only when a later request happens to land back on that same replica - about 1 in 4 times - while the other 3 in 4 requests still return PERSISTED_QUERY_NOT_FOUND. That is the arithmetic source of the observed ~75% miss rate.
A rolling restart clears the in-memory `Map` on whichever pod cycles, erasing every hash that pod had learned and forcing a fresh miss storm across the fleet as clients re-register from scratch.

The fix has to match the registry's storage to the unit of deployment (the whole fleet) rather than the unit of a single process. Apollo Server's `persistedQueries.cache` accepts any object implementing `get`/`set`/`delete`, so the storage backend is a drop-in swap that requires no resolver code changes.

Backing the registry with a shared store such as Redis (for example `apollo-server-cache-redis`'s `RedisCache`), combined with a TTL so the registry doesn't grow unbounded, makes a registration visible to every replica and lets it survive any single pod restarting.

For first-party clients, generating a hash-to-query manifest at build time and shipping it with the client (trusted documents) goes further: the server never accepts an arbitrary client-supplied registration at all, which removes both the miss storm and the open registration attack surface in one move.

Validating the fix requires more than reading the diff: the `PERSISTED_QUERY_NOT_FOUND` rate should fall to near zero at steady state, average request payload should shrink to hash-size, a rolling-restart soak should confirm registrations survive pod churn, and the Redis-backed store itself should be load-tested so its added network hop doesn't become the new bottleneck.
Design uses the Relay Connection model: posts(page: { first, after }) returns a PostConnection { edges { cursor, node }, pageInfo { endCursor, hasNextPage }, totalCount }.

Reason for the Connection → edges → node shape instead of a flat array: edge exists to attach a coordinate (cursor) to each element, and pageInfo is the minimal state the client needs to loop — it only keeps the previous endCursor and stops once hasNextPage is false, never needing total count or an absolute index.

The cursor encodes a stable attribute (createdAt, with id as a tie-breaker when timestamps collide) then base64-encodes it so to the client it is opaque — the client must never guess its format, only echo it back verbatim, letting the server change the encoding later without breaking clients.
first is always clamped by the server to a MAX_PAGE_SIZE so a client cannot demand a giant page, with a sensible default page size applied when first is omitted.
after is exactly the previous page's endCursor.
Page-boundary semantics: an empty page returns endCursor: null and hasNextPage: false; the last page still carries a valid endCursor but hasNextPage: false, so the client knows to stop.
totalCount is optional — only add it if the cost of counting the full dataset is acceptable, since on a large store that count can be expensive.

Failure contract: an after cursor that cannot be decoded or points at a deleted record throws a typed exception that becomes the unified envelope with a stable code, INVALID_CURSOR — the server never silently guesses an approximate page, and this code tells the client to restart pagination from the beginning.
Event surface: a distinct subscription field per event type (postCreated, postUpdated), each pushing a payload named exactly after that field.

Decision to push the full node rather than just an id: the trade is a heavier frame but the client can render immediately with no refetch (fits an instant-feeling feed); id-only is lighter but forces a follow-up query, adding latency.
Write path: the mutation, as part of the write itself, publishes an event onto its own topic (e.g. POST_CREATED/POST_UPDATED).

The subscription resolver produces no data of its own — it only returns that topic's asyncIterator, so the mutation neither knows nor cares how many subscribers are listening (producer/consumer fully decoupled).

Transport: a persistent WebSocket channel in the graphql-ws protocol on the same endpoint as HTTP, which beats polling on latency, request volume, and true push semantics rather than fake-realtime polling.

Connection hygiene: keep-alive/ping-pong detects and reaps a connection whose client has already dropped (otherwise it hangs as a zombie connection eating resources), and an explicit unsubscribe releases the listener when a client leaves.

Reconnect/backfill: a push channel has no replay, so on reconnect the client re-subscribes for the future AND calls posts(after: last-seen-cursor) to backfill exactly the missed window, deduplicating by id at the seam between the backfilled batch and the live stream.

Named constraint: an in-process PubSub only publishes/receives within one instance — with multiple replicas an event on instance A never reaches a subscriber on instance B, requiring an external bus (e.g. Redis pubsub) for multi-instance, though that is an explicit extension, not the focus of this design.

Root problem: errors are shaped ad hoc at every throw site instead of through one place, so each failure looks different and the client resorts to parsing message strings — brittle and risks leaking a stack trace.
Fix: route every error through a single central mapping point (an exception filter on Nest/Spring/ASP.NET, or an error presenter on gqlgen).
That central point always emits the same envelope: { message, path, extensions.code }.
Typed domain exceptions carry their own stable code (e.g. BOOK_NOT_FOUND, VALIDATION_FAILED) through that point untouched.

Anything that is NOT a typed domain exception collapses to a generic INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR with the real message hidden from the client (though still logged server-side) — no stack trace ever reaches the response.
Client payoff: consumers branch on extensions.code instead of parsing message — a stable constant that survives a wording change.

GraphQL-specific nuance: a response can carry data and errors together (a resolver field fails while sibling fields still resolve), so a stable code per errors[] entry is what makes that partial failure consumable.

Offset counts an absolute position, so when a new element is inserted at the head between two loads, every position after it shifts back by one — the next page (at the old offset) ends up either repeating an item just seen or skipping one, depending on whether the insert lands before or inside the window being read; this isn't a bug in any one query, it's the inevitable consequence of paginating by "counting from the start."

Cursor pagination fixes the root cause by anchoring to a STABLE ATTRIBUTE of a specific element — say, its creation timestamp or id — instead of a countable index; "give me the elements after this element" stays correct no matter how many new posts were inserted ahead of it.
The client persists exactly one thing between requests: pageInfo.endCursor, sent back as the after argument on the next call — no total count, no absolute index required.
pageInfo.hasNextPage is the sole signal that tells the pagination loop to stop: fetch a page, read endCursor, send it back as after, repeat until hasNextPage is false.
The reason edge wraps node is so every element carries its own cursor along with it, while pageInfo acts as the steering wheel for the whole loop.

Close the loop with the error contract: a cursor that can't be decoded, or that points at an element which has since vanished, must not silently return a guessed page — it must throw an error with a stable code (e.g. INVALID_CURSOR) so the client knows for certain it has to refetch from the top instead of continuing to scroll on wrong data.

A field on type Query is allowed to execute in parallel and is assumed pure/cacheable by default; a field on type Mutation is guaranteed by the spec to run serially in declaration order, precisely because the engine knows it has a side effect.

When a write is registered as a query "for convenience," it inherits read guarantees it cannot honour: a caching or prefetching layer (e.g. a client auto-firing a query on link hover, or a persisted query) may unknowingly re-invoke that operation multiple times, believing it safe to retry.
If two such fields sit in the same selection set, the engine is free to run them in parallel, racing two writes against the same data.

The operation type is a CONTRACT read not just by humans but by machines — clients, caches, and codegen generate types from that assumption — so a write hidden under a read silently breaks the contract, surfacing not as an immediate error but later as duplicated or wrong data.
The rule: every side effect belongs on type Mutation.
A mutation should return the newly-written representation (e.g. createBook returning the book just created) so the client gets write+read in one round-trip.
The teammate's "convenience" argument isn't wrong about the feeling, but the cost is silent, hard-to-reproduce bugs — no production situation is worth that trade.
